mainTopic: Seriousness, preparation, and proper form in prayer
overview: The amud opens with stories of Sages who sobered wedding celebrations that had grown too wild, by breaking costly cups or singing about death. רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, then forbids filling one's mouth with laughter in this world, and ריש לקיש lived by this. Next comes a ברייתא about preparing for תפילה: begin from a settled הלכה, and the גמרא gives three examples. Another ברייתא says to approach תפילה with the joy of a מצוה, and to part from a friend with a matter of הלכה, illustrated by a teaching shared during a farewell walk. The amud then teaches about כוונה, the prayer habits of רבי עקיבא, and many rules learned from the verses about דניאל, דוד, חנה, and שלמה. These rules cover praying three set times a day, facing ירושלים, praying quietly, and putting praise before requests. רב המנונא draws four more rules from חנה's prayer. The amud ends as רבי אלעזר begins a lesson from עלי's rebuke of חנה, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: A costly cup interrupts the celebration
steps.stepSummary: The passage finishes an earlier wedding story: someone breaks an expensive cup, and the guests become sad.
steps.simpleTranslation: He brought a costly cup worth four hundred זוז, broke it in front of them, and they became sad.
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes a story that began on the previous amud. Breaking the cup changes the guests’ mood.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The price makes the loss noticeable. The text reports the guests’ sadness but does not name the person who broke the cup in this line.

phrases.aramaic: אַיְּיתִי כָּסָא דְמוֹקְרָא בַּת אַרְבַּע מְאָה זוּזִי,
phrases.english: He brought an expensive cup worth four hundred zuz,
and broke it before them, and they became sad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues a story on the previous amud.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A costly breakage changes the guests’ mood.

steps.title: רב אשי breaks a white-glass cup
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי sees excessive merriment at his son’s wedding and breaks a glass cup before the Sages.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי made a wedding celebration for his son. He saw the Sages enjoying themselves very much, brought a white-glass cup, broke it before them, and they became sad.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another wedding story with the same kind of interruption. This time it names רב אשי and says that he saw the Sages becoming very merry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first story reported the breakage and its effect. This story adds what רב אשי noticed before breaking the cup: the Sages’ unusually high spirits.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi made a wedding celebration for his son,

phrases.aramaic: חֲזַנְהוּ לְרַבָּנַן דַּהֲווֹ קָא בָדְחִי טוּבָא.
phrases.english: and saw the Sages, who were being very merry.
He brought a white-glass cup,
and broke it before them, and they became sad.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies a second example of a broken cup changing the mood.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב אשי interrupts unusually intense wedding merriment by breaking a cup.

steps.title: The Sages ask for a song
steps.stepSummary: At another wedding, the Sages ask רב המנונא זוטי to lead them in song.
steps.simpleTranslation: At the wedding of מר, son of רבינא, the Sages said to רב המנונא זוטי: Let the master begin a song for us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new wedding scene. The Sages’ request sets up what רב המנונא זוטי will choose to sing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No cup is broken in this scene. Instead, the next move will show how a song can change the mood.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַב הַמְנוּנָא זוּטֵי
phrases.english: The Sages said to Rav Hamnuna Zuti
at the wedding of Mar, son of Ravina:
Let the master begin for us.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּנַן לְרַב הַמְנוּנָא זוּטֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens another wedding example, now centered on a song.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Sages invite רב המנונא זוטי to begin singing.

steps.title: He sings about mortality
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא זוטי answers the request with a repeated line about death.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Woe to us, for we will die. Woe to us, for we will die.
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא זוטי responds with a sobering song rather than a festive one. He repeats its opening line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words bring mortality into the celebration. This is a different way of interrupting merriment from the broken cups in the earlier stories.

phrases.english: He said to them: Woe to us, for we will die.
Woe to us, for we will die.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the request for a song.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב המנונא זוטי begins a song about mortality.

steps.title: The Sages ask what to sing back
steps.stepSummary: The Sages ask רב המנונא זוטי for their response in the song.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said to him: What should we answer after you?
steps.whatsHappening: The Sages ask for the line they should say after his line. The גמרא is setting up his answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: They do not challenge his words here. They ask how to take part in the song he has begun.

phrases.aramaic: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ: אֲנַן מָה נַעֲנֵי בָּתְרָךְ?
phrases.english: They said to him: What shall we answer after you?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמְרִי לֵיהּ: אֲנַן מָה נַעֲנֵי בָּתְרָךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the response to the song’s opening line.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What should the Sages say after רב המנונא זוטי sings?

steps.title: He supplies the response
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא זוטי gives the Sages a line asking where the protecting תורה and מצוה are.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: Where is the תורה, and where is the מצוה, that protect us?
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא זוטי gives them the words to answer. Their line asks about the תורה and מצוה that protect them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The response continues the song’s serious tone. It is phrased as a question; the passage does not say that תורה and מצוה have no protective value.

phrases.english: He said to them: Where is the Torah,
and where is the commandment that protect us?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the words the Sages asked for.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They should answer with a question about the תורה and מצוה that protect them.

steps.title: A rule against unrestrained laughter
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, citing רבי שמעון בן יוחאי, forbids filling one’s mouth with laughter in this world and cites a verse.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי: A person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world, as it says: “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter and our tongue with song.”
steps.whatsHappening: The passage moves from wedding stories to an explicit rule. רבי יוחנן cites רבי שמעון בן יוחאי and introduces a verse to support it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule concerns filling one’s mouth with laughter, not every expression of happiness. The word “then” in the verse points toward a time still to be identified.

keyTerms.meaning: the Sage רבי שמעון בן יוחאי

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai:

phrases.aramaic: אָסוּר לְאָדָם שֶׁיְּמַלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: It is forbidden for a person to fill his mouth with laughter in this world,
as it is stated: “Then our mouth will be filled with laughter
and our tongue with song.”

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from examples of sobering a celebration to a stated rule about laughter.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person may not fill his mouth with laughter in this world.
steps.whyThisMatters: This gives an explicit rule after the three wedding scenes.

steps.title: The verse identifies when
steps.stepSummary: The passage explains when the verse’s promised fullness of laughter will occur.
steps.simpleTranslation: When? When they say among the nations, “The Lord has done great things for these people.”
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן's quotation of רבי שמעון בן יוחאי continues by asking when the verse’s “then” will be. It answers with the next words of the verse, which describe a future public recognition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The quoted words supply the time frame for the preceding verse. They explain why its full laughter is not presented as the ordinary state of the present world.

phrases.english: When? At the time when “they will say among the nations,
The Lord has done great things for these.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the time indicated by “then” in the quoted verse.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The fullness of laughter belongs to the time described by the nations’ declaration.

steps.title: ריש לקיש follows the teaching
steps.stepSummary: A report says that ריש לקיש stopped filling his mouth with laughter after hearing the teaching from רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: They said about ריש לקיש that, from the time he heard it from his teacher רבי יוחנן, he never filled his mouth with laughter in this world.
steps.whatsHappening: The passage ends with an account of how ריש לקיש acted after hearing the rule. His conduct gives a concrete example of following it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The report is about what ריש לקיש did from the time he heard רבי יוחנן’s teaching. It does not say that he never experienced happiness.
steps.whatToRemember: The stories show celebrations being sobered; the later teaching specifically restricts filling one’s mouth with laughter in this world.

phrases.english: They said about Reish Lakish

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁמִּיָּמָיו לֹא מִלֵּא שְׂחוֹק פִּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה,
phrases.english: that he never filled his mouth with laughter in this world,
from when he heard it from his teacher, Rabbi Yoḥanan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the passage with an example of the rule being followed.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: After hearing רבי יוחנן’s teaching, ריש לקיש did not fill his mouth with laughter in this world.

steps.title: Begin prayer after a settled ruling
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים distinguish between absorbing legal discussion and a clear, settled ruling before תְּפִלָּה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: One should not stand up to pray directly from a legal case or from discussion of a point of הֲלָכָה, but from a settled הֲלָכָה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a rule about what a person should be doing just before תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Working through a case or deciding a legal question can keep a person's mind busy. A settled ruling provides learning without leaving that question open.

keyTerms.meaning: a matter of Jewish law under discussion

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One should not stand up to pray
directly from a legal case,
nor directly from discussion of a matter of law,
but from a settled legal ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the report about ריש לקיש, the גמרא turns to a teaching about preparation for תְּפִלָּה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Begin תְּפִלָּה after a settled הֲלָכָה, not directly from a case or a legal discussion.

steps.title: What counts as a settled ruling?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a concrete example of the kind of ruling just mentioned.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is an example of a settled הֲלָכָה?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks what the rule in the previous step means in practice. This sets up the examples that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The instruction names a type of learning but gives no example. The question asks the speakers to identify one.

keyTerms.meaning: is it like; what does it look like

phrases.english: And what is an example of a settled legal ruling?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: It asks for an example of the ruling named in step 10.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A concrete example of הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה.

steps.title: אביי gives an example about counting clean days
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers with a ruling reported by רבי זירא: even a very small sighting of blood leads to counting seven clean days.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: An example is the teaching of רבי זירא. רבי זירא said: The daughters of Israel adopted a stricter practice for themselves: even if they see a drop of blood as small as a mustard seed, they count seven clean days for it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי supplies the first example of a settled הֲלָכָה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא describes a practice the women accepted upon themselves. אביי uses that stated practice as an example of a ruling one can learn before תְּפִלָּה.

keyTerms.meaning: as small as a mustard seed

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר אַבָּיֵי: כִּי הָא דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא,
phrases.english: Abaye said: Like this teaching of Rabbi Zeira,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי זֵירָא: בְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל הֶחֱמִירוּ עַל עַצְמָן,
phrases.english: for Rabbi Zeira said: The daughters of Israel adopted a stricter practice for themselves,
so that even if they see a drop of blood as small as a mustard seed,
they count seven clean days for it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר אַבָּיֵי: כִּי הָא דְּרַבִּי זֵירָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It gives the first example requested in step 11.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The practice reported by רבי זירא is an example of הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה.

steps.title: רבא gives an example about grain brought in with its chaff
steps.stepSummary: רבא offers another example: רב הושעיא describes grain brought in with its chaff for an animal to eat, which is exempt from מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: An example is the teaching of רב הושעיא. רב הושעיא said: A person may arrange matters with his grain and bring it in with its chaff, so that his animal can eat it, and it is exempt from מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a second example in answer to the same question. He is adding an example, not challenging אביי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This example concerns grain brought in while still in its chaff for an animal to eat. The stated exemption from מעשר applies to that described arrangement; the passage does not say that all grain is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: arranges matters by a permitted workaround

steps.whatToRemember: Both אביי and רבא are answering the same question by giving examples of הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה.

phrases.aramaic: רָבָא אָמַר, כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא,
phrases.english: Rava said: Like this teaching of Rav Hoshaya,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא: מַעֲרִים אָדָם עַל תְּבוּאָתוֹ
phrases.english: for Rav Hoshaya said: A person may use a workaround with his grain
and bring it in with its chaff,
so that his animal can eat it,
and it is exempt from tithes.

steps.triggerLanguage: רָבָא אָמַר, כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: It adds a different example to אביי's answer without rejecting it.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The grain arrangement taught by רב הושעיא is another example of הֲלָכָה פְּסוּקָה.

steps.title: One more example of a settled ruling
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא adds a ruling about blood drawn from a consecrated animal as another example for the earlier question.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or, if you wish, take this teaching of רב הונא, who said in the name of רבי זעירא: If someone draws blood from a consecrated animal, benefiting from the blood is forbidden, and the law of misuse of consecrated property applies to it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers another answer to the earlier request for a concrete ruling to consider before תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is an additional example, not a challenge to the examples already given. The ruling addresses blood drawn from a consecrated animal: one may not benefit from it, and misuse of consecrated property applies.

keyTerms.meaning: and if you wish, say; introduces another answer
misuse of consecrated property applies to it

phrases.aramaic: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא,
phrases.english: And if you wish, say: like this teaching of Rav Huna,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַב הוּנָא, אָמַר רַבִּי זְעֵירָא:
phrases.english: for Rav Huna said that Rabbi Zeira said:
One who draws blood from a consecrated animal—
benefit from it is forbidden, and the law of misuse of consecrated property applies to it.
phrases.notes: The two rulings concern the blood that was drawn.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא, כִּי הָא דְּרַב הוּנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a third example in answer to the question addressed by steps 12 and 13.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ruling about blood drawn from a consecrated animal is another concrete example of a settled ruling.

steps.title: Two practices before prayer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא reports that the חכמים followed the משנה, while רב אשי followed the earlier ברייתא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים acted according to our משנה; רב אשי acted according to the ברייתא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves from examples of rulings to how people actually prepared for תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The חכמים followed the משנה’s direction to approach תְּפִלָּה with seriousness. רב אשי followed the earlier ברייתא about beginning from a settled ruling; this is not yet the new ברייתא introduced in the next step.

phrases.english: The Sages acted according to our mishna;
Rav Ashi acted according to the baraita.
phrases.notes: This points back to the earlier teaching about a settled ruling.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the final example of a ruling to a report of practices before prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The חכמים followed the משנה’s preparation for תְּפִלָּה, while רב אשי followed the earlier ברייתא’s preparation.

steps.title: Approach prayer with the joy of a מצוה
steps.stepSummary: A new ברייתא lists states of mind to avoid before תְּפִלָּה and names the joy of a מצוה as the proper starting point.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: One should not stand to pray out of sadness, laziness, laughter, conversation, frivolity, or idle matters, but out of the joy of a מצוה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא introduces a new ברייתא about the state of mind with which a person begins תְּפִלָּה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The list rules out both heavy distraction, such as sadness, and light distraction, such as joking or idle talk. It replaces them with joy connected to a מצוה, not just any cheerful mood.

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One should not stand to pray

phrases.aramaic: לֹא מִתּוֹךְ עַצְבוּת, וְלֹא מִתּוֹךְ עַצְלוּת,
phrases.english: not out of sadness and not out of laziness,

phrases.aramaic: וְלֹא מִתּוֹךְ שְׂחוֹק, וְלֹא מִתּוֹךְ שִׂיחָה,
phrases.english: and not out of laughter and not out of conversation,
and not out of frivolity,
and not out of idle matters,
but out of the joy of a מצוה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Introduces a new teaching on preparation for prayer, rather than explaining the earlier ברייתא followed by רב אשי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Begin תְּפִלָּה from שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה, not from the listed distracting states.

steps.title: Part from a friend after meaningful talk
steps.stepSummary: The same ברייתא applies a similar pattern to taking leave of another person: end with a matter of הלכה rather than idle talk.
steps.simpleTranslation: Similarly, a person should not take leave of a friend out of conversation, laughter, frivolity, or idle matters, but out of a matter of הלכה.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא extends its advice about a good starting point for תְּפִלָּה to a good ending for a conversation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The shared idea is to make the moment of transition meaningful. Here the positive instruction is to part after discussing a matter of הלכה; it is not a repetition of the rule about beginning תְּפִלָּה.

phrases.english: And similarly, a person should not take leave of his friend

phrases.aramaic: לֹא מִתּוֹךְ שִׂיחָה, וְלֹא מִתּוֹךְ שְׂחוֹק,
phrases.english: not out of conversation and not out of laughter,
and not out of frivolity,
and not out of idle matters,
but out of a matter of halakha.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies the ברייתא’s concern for a meaningful transition to parting from a friend.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When parting from another person, finish with a דְּבַר הֲלָכָה rather than idle talk.

steps.title: An example of ending with meaningful words
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא points to the early prophets, whose words concluded with praise and consolation.
steps.simpleTranslation: For so we find among the early prophets: they concluded their words with words of praise and consolation.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא supports its advice about parting by pointing to an example of a meaningful ending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cited endings contain praise and consolation, not an explicit statement of הלכה. They support the broader point that final words should carry substance rather than be idle talk.
steps.whatToRemember: The example from the נביאים supports ending with meaningful words; it does not say their closing words were themselves דְּבַר הֲלָכָה.

phrases.english: For so we find among the early prophets,
that they concluded their words with words of praise and consolation.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers an example to support the instruction about how to end an interaction.
steps.raayaObject: The value of ending with meaningful words.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The practice attributed to the נביאים הראשונים of concluding with praise and consolation.

steps.title: A teaching about how to take leave
steps.stepSummary: מָרִי teaches that people should part while discussing הֲלָכָה, because that conversation will help one remember the other.
steps.simpleTranslation: מָרִי taught likewise: A person should take leave of another only while discussing a matter of הֲלָכָה, because through it he will remember him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second teaching to the earlier advice about taking leave. This version gives a reason: the matter of הֲלָכָה helps one person remember the other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous teaching said what kind of conversation to have when parting. This one adds what that conversation accomplishes afterward: it leaves a lasting reminder.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן תְּנָא מָרִי בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא:
phrases.english: And so taught Mari, the grandson of Rav Huna, son of Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba:

phrases.aramaic: אַל יִפָּטֵר אָדָם מֵחֲבֵירוֹ אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ דְּבַר הֲלָכָה,
phrases.english: A person should take leave of another only while discussing a matter of law,
because through that he remembers him.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן תְּנָא מָרִי בַּר בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב הוּנָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יִרְמְיָה בַּר אַבָּא:
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns from the example of the prophets to the earlier instruction about taking leave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Take leave while discussing a matter of הֲלָכָה, so the other person will remember you.

steps.title: A question during a farewell journey
steps.stepSummary: רַב כָּהֲנָא accompanies רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי and asks him about an old saying concerning the palm trees of בָּבֶל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב כָּהֲנָא accompanied רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי from פּוּם נַהֲרָא to the palm grove of בָּבֶל. When they arrived, he asked what people meant when they said that those palm trees had been there since אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins an example of a conversation during an accompaniment. רַב כָּהֲנָא raises a question that sets up the teaching in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is about a local saying, not yet about a verse or a rule. It gives רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי an opening to share a teaching.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הָא דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא אַלְוְיֵיהּ לְרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי
phrases.english: As in this case: Rav Kahana accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi

phrases.aramaic: מִפּוּם נַהֲרָא עַד בֵּי צִנְיָתָא דְּבָבֶל.
phrases.english: from Pum Nahara to the palm grove of Babylonia.
When he reached there, he said to him:
Master, is what people say really so:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי צִנְיָתָא דְּבָבֶל אִיתַנְהוּ מֵאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְעַד הַשְׁתָּא?
phrases.english: These palm trees of Babylonia have been here from Adam the first man until now?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָא דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא אַלְוְיֵיהּ לְרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Begins a concrete example of the parting conversation just recommended.

steps.title: A verse seems to repeat itself
steps.stepSummary: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי recalls a teaching of רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא, which asks why a verse says that no one settled in a land after saying that no one passed through it.
steps.simpleTranslation: He replied, “You reminded me of something רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא said.” The teaching asks about the verse, “In a land through which no man passed and where no person settled”: If no one passed through it, how could anyone have settled there?
steps.whatsHappening: רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי turns the question about the palm trees into a question about a verse. He challenges what the verse’s second description adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If nobody even passed through the land, saying that nobody settled there sounds unnecessary. That difficulty prepares the explanation that follows.

keyTerms.meaning: what does the written verse mean?

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַדְכַּרְתַּן מִילְּתָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: He said to him: You reminded me of a teaching of Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹסֵי בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
phrases.english: for Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Hanina, said: What does it mean that it is written,
“In a land through which no man passed
and where no person settled”?

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּלֹא עָבַר הֵיאַךְ יָשַׁב?
phrases.english: But if no one passed through, how could anyone have settled?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מֵאַחַר דְּלֹא עָבַר הֵיאַךְ יָשַׁב?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The question about the local saying prompts a teaching that begins with a difficulty in a verse.
steps.kashyaTarget: The apparent repetition in the verse’s descriptions of the uninhabited land.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If no one passed through, saying that no one settled there seems to add nothing.

steps.title: The verse points to a decree about settlement
steps.stepSummary: The teaching explains the verse through אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן: land he designated for settlement became settled, while land he did not designate remained unsettled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the verse teaches you: Every land that אדם הראשון decreed should be settled was settled, and every land that he did not decree should be settled was not settled.
steps.whatsHappening: The teaching answers the difficulty in the verse. It gives “אָדָם” a particular meaning here: אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן and his decree about where people would settle.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second description is no longer just a repeat of “no man passed through.” It conveys a separate idea about whether the land was designated for settlement. This also answers רַב כָּהֲנָא's question: the saying about the palm trees of בָּבֶל means the land was designated for them from the time of אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, so the parting conversation ended with a teaching.

phrases.english: Rather, it comes to tell you: Every land

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁגָּזַר עָלֶיהָ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן לְיִשּׁוּב — נִתְיַשְּׁבָה.
phrases.english: that Adam the first man decreed should be settled was settled.
And every land that he did not decree
Adam the first man should be settled was not settled.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers why the verse includes the words about a person settling there.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reads the verse’s mention of אָדָם as introducing a distinct teaching about אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The statement that no person settled there appeared redundant.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wording teaches that settlement follows what אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן decreed.

steps.title: Another long accompaniment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא records how far רַב מָרְדְּכַי accompanied רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי, with two versions of the destination.
steps.simpleTranslation: רַב מָרְדְּכַי accompanied רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי from הַגְרוֹנְיָא to בֵּי כֵיפֵי; some say he accompanied him as far as בֵּי דוּרָא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another account of accompanying רַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי. It reports two versions of where the journey ended.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This account returns to the action of accompanying someone. Unlike the previous story, it does not report a conversation or a new teaching during the walk.

keyTerms.meaning: the destination in the first version
the destination in the second version

steps.whatToRemember: The first journey shows a conversation leading to a teaching; this line adds a separate example of accompanying someone.

phrases.aramaic: רַב מָרְדְּכַי אַלְוְיֵיהּ לְרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי מֵהַגְרוֹנְיָא,
phrases.english: Rav Mordekhai accompanied Rav Shimi bar Ashi from Hagronya,
as far as Bei Keifei.
And some say: as far as Bei Dura.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב מָרְדְּכַי אַלְוְיֵיהּ לְרַב שִׁימִי בַּר אָשֵׁי מֵהַגְרוֹנְיָא,
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the explanation of the verse and adds another accompaniment account.

steps.title: Direct the heart toward Heaven
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים require a person praying to focus the heart toward Heaven, and אבא שאול points to a verse as a sign of this.
steps.simpleTranslation: The חכמים taught: One who prays must direct the heart toward Heaven. אבא שאול says a sign of this is the verse, “Prepare their heart; Your ear will listen.”
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a teaching about the attention needed during prayer. אבא שאול then connects that teaching to a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The instruction concerns the person’s inner focus, not a particular posture. The verse places preparation of the heart beside God’s listening.

keyTerms.meaning: that one should direct or focus

phrases.english: The Sages taught: One who prays must
direct his heart toward Heaven.
Abba Shaul says: A sign of this is,
“Prepare their heart; Your ear will listen.”

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the account of accompanying someone, the גמרא turns to guidance about prayer.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person praying must direct the heart toward Heaven.

steps.title: Public and private prayer look different
steps.stepSummary: רבי עקיבא prayed briefly with the congregation to avoid burdening them, but his private prayer included many bows and prostrations.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה taught that רבי עקיבא shortened his prayer with the congregation because he did not want to burden them. When alone, he bowed and prostrated so much that someone could leave him in one corner and find him in another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא describes how רבי עקיבא prayed in two settings. It then explains why he appeared to move across the room during private prayer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With the congregation, his concern was not to keep others waiting. Alone, his many bows and prostrations caused the movement described.

phrases.english: It was taught; Rabbi Yehuda said:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ הָיָה מִנְהָגוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא,
phrases.english: This was Rabbi Akiva’s practice:
When he prayed with the congregation—

phrases.aramaic: הָיָה מְקַצֵּר וְעוֹלֶה, מִפְּנֵי טוֹרַח צִבּוּר.
phrases.english: he would shorten his prayer and finish, because of the burden on the congregation.
But when he prayed by himself—
someone would leave him in one corner,
and find him in another corner.
And why did he move so much?
Because of bows and prostrations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא moves from a general teaching about prayer to an account of how רבי עקיבא prayed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי עקיבא shortened public prayer to avoid burdening the congregation, while his private prayer involved extensive bowing and prostration.

steps.title: Pray in a room with windows
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא says to pray in a house with windows and points to the description of דניאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said: A person should always pray in a house with windows, as the verse says, “And he had open windows,” and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another instruction about prayer, this time about the room. It supports the instruction with a verse describing דניאל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new detail is the presence of windows. The quoted words point to דניאל’s open windows; the source here does not spell out further requirements about them.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba said:

phrases.aramaic: לְעוֹלָם יִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם בְּבַיִת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ חַלּוֹנוֹת,
phrases.english: A person should always pray in a house that has windows,
as it is stated: “And he had open windows,” and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא leaves the account of רבי עקיבא and introduces guidance drawn from דניאל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A person should pray in a house with windows.

steps.title: Could a person pray all day?
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא raises the possibility of praying throughout the entire day, setting up the next line’s answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: Could a person pray all day long?
steps.whatsHappening: A ברייתא begins a series of 'יָכוֹל' (I might have thought) suggestions, each rejected by a verse. The first asks whether prayer could take place throughout the whole day, which sets up an answer from דניאל’s practice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The previous verse supplied guidance about place. The גמרא now turns to a different detail: the pattern of prayer during the day.

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם כׇּל הַיּוֹם כּוּלּוֹ —
phrases.english: Could a person pray all day long—

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם כׇּל הַיּוֹם כּוּלּוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא continues drawing guidance from דניאל, shifting from the place of prayer to its daily pattern.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a person could pray throughout the entire day.

steps.title: דניאל’s three daily times provide the answer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the all-day possibility by citing the verse’s description of דניאל praying three times.
steps.simpleTranslation: This has already been made clear through דניאל: “And three times,” and so on.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by pointing to דניאל’s three daily prayer times. The verse supplies a set pattern rather than the proposed all-day pattern.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer uses another part of the account of דניאל, not the windows quoted above. It addresses the question of a daily pattern; this line does not discuss the rules for additional voluntary prayers.

phrases.english: It has already been made clear through Daniel:
“And three times,” and so on.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This supplies the verse-based answer to the possibility raised in step 27.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: דניאל’s practice is described as occurring three times, giving prayer a set daily pattern.
steps.whatToRemember: From דניאל we have learned two details so far: windows for the place of prayer, and three set times for its daily pattern. The ברייתא continues with more details in the next steps.

steps.title: Maybe this practice only began in exile?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises the idea that דניאל's practice of praying three times a day only started once he was exiled to Babylonia.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that this practice only began when he came to the exile.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא suggests a possible mistaken idea: maybe דניאל only started fixed prayer after he was exiled. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse describes דניאל praying in בבל, so a reader might think fixed prayer was a new response to גלות. The ברייתא raises this only so it can reject it with the next words of the verse.

keyTerms.meaning: 'I might have thought.' It opens a possible but mistaken reading that is about to be rejected.

steps.confusionAlert: 'יָכוֹל' is not anyone's real opinion. It is a test idea that the ברייתא raises only so a verse can rule it out.

phrases.english: I might have thought that from when he came to the exile it began

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the series of 'יָכוֹל' questions about the verse describing דניאל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Did fixed prayer three times daily begin only with the Babylonian exile?

steps.title: He had done so before
steps.stepSummary: The verse says דניאל prayed 'as he had done before', so the practice existed before the exile.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has already been stated: 'just as he had done before this.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question by quoting the end of the verse: דניאל was continuing what he had always done.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'מִן קַדְמַת דְּנָא' show that this was an old habit and not a new practice of exile. So fixed prayer is not a product of גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: It has already been stated (in the verse)

phrases.english: It was already stated:
"As he had done before this."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The verse says דניאל prayed as he had done before, so the practice existed before the exile.

steps.title: Maybe one may pray facing any direction?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises the idea that a person may face any direction he wants when praying.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that a person may pray toward any direction he wishes.
steps.whatsHappening: A new 'יָכוֹל' raises the possibility that direction does not matter in תפילה. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since prayer is about the heart, one might assume direction is irrelevant. The ברייתא raises this so it can show from the verse that there is a set direction.

keyTerms.meaning: Direction (literally 'wind', as in a compass direction)

phrases.aramaic: יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם לְכׇל רוּחַ שֶׁיִּרְצֶה —
phrases.english: I might have thought a person may pray toward any direction he wishes

steps.triggerLanguage: יָכוֹל יִתְפַּלֵּל אָדָם לְכׇל רוּחַ שֶׁיִּרְצֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new detail learned from the same verse about דניאל.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is there a required direction for תפילה?

steps.title: Face ירושלים
steps.stepSummary: The verse says דניאל's windows were open 'facing ירושלים', so one prays toward ירושלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: The verse teaches: 'facing ירושלים.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers from the verse: דניאל's windows faced ירושלים, so prayer is directed there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The detail about the windows is not just background. It teaches the הלכה that a person faces ירושלים when praying.

keyTerms.meaning: 'The verse teaches.' It introduces the source that answers a 'יָכוֹל'.
Facing (Aramaic). This printed reading is corrected to נֶגֶד, the verse's actual word.

steps.whyThisMatters: This is a source for the practical הלכה of facing ירושלים during תפילה.

phrases.english: The verse states: "facing Jerusalem."
phrases.notes: Brackets show a text correction: the verse (Daniel 6:11) reads נֶגֶד.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 31.

steps.title: Maybe all three prayers can be said at once?
steps.stepSummary: Since דניאל only says 'three times', the ברייתא raises the idea that all three could be said together.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that one may combine them all at one time.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks whether the three daily prayers could be said one after another at a single time. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verse about דניאל gives the number (three) but not the times. So the ברייתא needs another source to show they must be spread out.

phrases.english: I might have thought he may include them all at one time

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on step 28's 'three times' and asks how they are spread out.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May the three daily prayers be said together at once?

steps.title: דוד: evening, morning, and noon
steps.stepSummary: דוד's verse lists evening, morning, and noon, so the three prayers are spread across the day.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has already been made clear by דוד, as it is written: 'Evening and morning and noon...'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא brings a verse from דוד in תהילים that names three separate times of day.
steps.deeperAnalysis: דניאל's verse gives the number three, and דוד's verse gives the timing. Together they teach that there are three prayers at three separate times: מעריב, שחרית, and מנחה.

phrases.english: It was already made explicit by David,
as it is written: "Evening and morning and noon, etc."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 33.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The three prayers must be spread out over evening, morning, and noon.

steps.title: Maybe one may pray out loud?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא raises the idea that a person may make his voice heard during תפילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that one may make his voice heard in his prayer.
steps.whatsHappening: The next 'יָכוֹל' asks whether one may pray aloud. This line sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The verses about דניאל say nothing about how loudly one prays, so the ברייתא needs another source. It raises the possibility of praying aloud only so that the next step can reject it from חנה.

phrases.english: I might have thought he may make his voice heard in his prayer

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new detail: the volume of prayer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May one pray the עמידה aloud?

steps.title: חנה: her voice was not heard
steps.stepSummary: From חנה, whose voice was not heard as she prayed, we learn that the עמידה is said quietly.
steps.simpleTranslation: It has already been made clear by חנה, as it is stated: 'and her voice was not heard.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers from חנה, who moved her lips but did not let her voice be heard.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חנה's prayer becomes the model for the עמידה. The lips move and the words are formed, but the voice is not made audible to others.

keyTerms.meaning: Hannah, mother of שמואל, whose prayer is a model for תפילה
And her voice was not heard

steps.whatToRemember: From these verses: fixed prayer existed before the exile (דניאל). Face ירושלים (דניאל). The three prayers are spread over evening, morning, and noon (דוד). Pray quietly (חנה).
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for saying the עמידה in a quiet voice.

phrases.english: It was already made explicit by Hannah,
as it is stated: "and her voice could not be heard."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 35.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: One does not make his voice heard in the עמידה, as we learn from חנה.

steps.title: Maybe requests should come before praise
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא suggests that a person might first ask for his needs and only afterward say praise.
steps.simpleTranslation: I might have thought that a person should first ask for his needs and only afterward pray.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא raises a possible idea about the order of תפילה. This sets up the next step, where the idea will be rejected from a verse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This uses the same 'יכול' pattern as the earlier steps about דניאל, דוד, and חנה. The question is about order: should requests come first, before the praise and thanks?

keyTerms.meaning: 'I might have thought', which opens a possible idea that will be checked
his needs, meaning his personal requests

phrases.english: I might think a person should ask for his needs
and afterward pray (praise)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Next item in the ברייתא's series of 'יכול' questions about how to pray
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a person ask for his needs before or after praising ה׳?

steps.title: שלמה's verse puts praise before requests
steps.stepSummary: The verse puts 'רנה' (praise) before 'תפילה' (request), so praise comes first.
steps.simpleTranslation: This was already made clear by שלמה, as it says: 'To hear the song and the prayer.' 'Song' means praise, and 'prayer' means request.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question with a verse from שלמה's prayer when the בית המקדש was dedicated. Praise is listed first, so praise is said first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof depends on how the two words are defined. 'רנה' is praise and thanks, and 'תפילה' here means asking for needs. Since the verse lists רנה first, requests come only after praise.

keyTerms.meaning: song, meaning praise and thanks to ה׳

steps.confusionAlert: In this verse the word 'תפילה' does not mean the whole prayer. It means only the requests. The praise part is called 'רנה'.

phrases.english: It was already made clear by Solomon,
as it says: 'To hear the song and the prayer.'
'Song' is prayer (praise),
'prayer' is request.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers and rejects the idea raised in step 37
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Praise comes first and requests come after, based on the order of the words in שלמה's verse.

steps.title: No requests before the עמידה, but unlimited requests after it
steps.stepSummary: No requests are said after אמת ויציב, but after the עמידה one may add even something as long as the וידוי of יום הכיפורים.
steps.simpleTranslation: A person does not say any request after 'אמת ויציב'. But after the תפילה, he may say even something like the order of the confession of יום הכיפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא turns the rule into practice: no requests in the gap before the עמידה, but full freedom after it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אמת ויציב leads straight into the עמידה, which opens with praise. So a request inserted there would come before the praise. Once the עמידה is finished, the praise has already been said, so a person may add requests of any length.

keyTerms.meaning: the ברכה after קריאת שמע of the morning, said right before the עמידה
confession, as said on יום הכיפורים
like the order or length of

steps.whatToRemember: Praise comes before requests. Do not add requests between אמת ויציב and the עמידה. After the עמידה, you may add as many requests as you want.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source for the custom of adding personal prayers after the עמידה, as in אלהי נצור and similar additions.

after 'Emet VeYatziv.'

steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Requests are not said before the עמידה, but they may be added without limit after it.

steps.title: רב says the same thing about requests after the עמידה
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that even though requests belong in שומע תפילה, one may add long requests after the עמידה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was also taught by an אמורא: רב חייא בר אשי said in the name of רב: Even though they said a person asks for his needs in 'שומע תפילה', if he wants to add them after his תפילה, he may say even something as long as the order of יום הכיפורים.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support from an אמורא, רב, who agrees with the ברייתא's ruling about adding requests after the עמידה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב adds a detail. Inside the עמידה, the place for personal requests is the ברכה of שומע תפילה. That rule does not limit him, though. After the עמידה he may add as much as he wants.

keyTerms.meaning: 'it was also stated', introducing an אמורא who teaches the same idea
the ברכה in the עמידה where personal requests may be added

steps.title: From חנה: pray with focus and move your lips
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא learns many הלכות from חנה, starting with כוונה and saying the words with the lips.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: How many important הלכות can be learned from these verses about חנה! 'And חנה was speaking in her heart' teaches that one who prays must focus his heart. 'Only her lips moved' teaches that one who prays must say the words with his lips.
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא opens a list of הלכות learned from the verse about חנה's prayer. Here he gives the first two.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each part of the verse teaches a separate rule. 'In her heart' teaches that real focus is needed. 'Her lips moved' teaches that thinking alone is not enough, and the words must actually be spoken.

keyTerms.meaning: that he forms the words clearly with his lips

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said:
How many important laws
can be learned from these verses of Hannah!
'And Hannah was speaking in her heart':
from here, one who prays must focus his heart.
'Only her lips moved':
from here, one who prays must say the words with his lips.

steps.triggerLanguage: כַּמָּה הִלְכְתָא גִּבָּרָווֹתָא אִיכָּא לְמִשְׁמַע מֵהָנֵי קְרָאֵי דְחַנָּה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new list of הלכות from חנה, building on the חנה proof used in step 36
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who prays must have כוונה and must say the words with his lips.

steps.title: From חנה: pray quietly, and a drunk person may not pray
steps.stepSummary: From the same verse: do not raise your voice in תפילה, and a שיכור may not pray.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And her voice was not heard' teaches that it is forbidden to raise one's voice in תפילה. 'And עלי thought she was drunk' teaches that a drunk person is forbidden to pray.
steps.whatsHappening: רב המנונא continues his list with two more הלכות from the verse about חנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule of praying quietly matches what the ברייתא taught in step 36. The last rule comes from עלי's reaction: he rebuked her only because a drunk person is not allowed to pray.

keyTerms.meaning: עלי הכהן, the כהן גדול who saw חנה praying

steps.whatToRemember: From חנה we learn four rules: pray with כוונה, say the words with your lips, do not raise your voice, and do not pray while drunk.

phrases.english: 'And her voice was not heard':
from here, it is forbidden to raise one's voice in his prayer.
'And Eli thought she was drunk':
from here, a drunk person is forbidden to pray.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב המנונא's list from step 41
steps.mimraCoreRuling: It is forbidden to raise one's voice in the עמידה, and a שיכור may not pray.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר begins a lesson from עלי's rebuke
steps.stepSummary: Quoting עלי's words to חנה, רבי אלעזר starts to teach a rule about someone who sees something in another person.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And עלי said to her: How long will you be drunk?' רבי אלעזר said: From here we learn that one who sees in his friend...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes עלי's rebuke of חנה, and רבי אלעזר begins to draw a lesson from it. This is a setup line, and the rest of his teaching continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The focus moves from what חנה did to what עלי did. רבי אלעזר is about to teach a rule about how to respond when you see something wrong in another person.

keyTerms.meaning: for one who sees in his friend (something wrong)

phrases.english: 'And Eli said to her:
How long will you be drunk, etc.'
Rabbi Elazar said:
From here, for one who sees in his friend

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from עלי thinking חנה was drunk to the words of his rebuke, opening a new teaching
